World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Students chasing hydrogen racing world title in Switzerland
World.content:
The Steel City was heralded as the Hydrogen Hub before the Whyalla Steelworks was forced into administration.

But now a group of high school students are taking Whyalla's hydrogen potential to the world stage.

For 17-year-old aspiring engineer Simon Coppins, it is a chance to see two years of "blood, sweat and tears" pay off.

Lead racer Simon Coppins aspires to be an engineer. (Supplied: Simon Coppins)

The H2 Grand Prix tasks competitors with building a hydrogen-powered RC car and completing the greatest number of laps in four hours.

According to team manager Caelan Kaminski, consistent lap times are the key to success.

"It's always about pacing yourself. We don't want to be the fastest car out there, because the fastest cars always run out of fuel the quickest," he said.

Team manager Caelan Kaminski. (ABC News: Arj Ganesan)

At the South Australian world qualifying event in 2025, the team was in first place by a heavy margin, but 30 minutes before the end, they were disqualified over a technical fault.

For lead driver Simon and his team, which had spent hundreds of hours perfecting their car, the outcome was heartbreaking.

The Whyalla team has spent hours building and working on its cars. (ABC News: Arj Ganesan)

"I just spent three hours and 30 minutes driving without blinking," he said.

"We were so close to our end goal."

According to race officials, the mistake came down to a simple misunderstanding, with the team swapping out one of its batteries during a mandatory maintenance check.

The RC cars are fuelled by hydrogen that the team produces. (ABC News: Arj Ganesan)

The team, which had established a dominating lead, did not need to make the switch and had they not done so, would have taken out first place.

Though they missed out on competing in Germany in 2025, fortune has given them another shot this year.

The race changed its scheduling format, hosting its world competition earlier in the year to better align with the northern hemisphere's calendar.

Going forward, qualifying events for countries in the Asia Pacific will be held the year before.

But as this decision was only made recently, qualifiers for the Switzerland competition could not be held in Australia.

Eli Coppins, Caelan Kaminski, Simon Coppins, Shannon Bayogos and Karman Randhawa practise ahead of their race in Switzerland. (ABC News: Arj Ganesan)

According to the organisers, several high-performing teams have subsequently been invited to the June meet, including Whyalla, as the team came so close to victory in 2025.

"It's definitely a big opportunity for all of us to prove Whyalla's worth and, you know, Whyalla's skills and community on a world stage," Caelan said.

The students have spent hours tinkering with their model cars to get them race ready. (ABC News: Arj Ganesan)

Sunrise Christian School science, technology, engineering, and mathematics teacher Trudi Wynn could not be prouder of how her students acted.

"They were very, very gracious in the disqualification," she said.

"It was obviously very disappointing.

"They were interacting with our sponsors and thanking them and apologising because they didn't obviously win.

"I think that they are an excellent representation of Whyalla."

Teacher Trudi Wynn praised the team for handling past setbacks with grace. (ABC News: Arj Ganesan)

Ms Wynn said the competition was a fantastic tool to inspire students to study STEM.

"This is why I'm a teacher," she said.

"My father was an inventor, so I'm very much into problem-solving and solving real-world problems and getting my students involved."

The team now needs to raise roughly $100,000 to cover the costs of return flights, accommodation, and equipment for the five students and five accompanying adults.

World.title: Iran fears captain may be denied entry to US for World Cup
World.content:
Iran's football federation said on Saturday the country "definitely" would participate in the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

However, they insisted that tournament hosts — the United States, Canada and Mexico — consider Tehran's concerns around the team's travel and how it will be treated.

"All players and technical staff, especially those who served their military service in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, should be granted visas without problems," Football Federation Islamic Republic of Iran president Mehdi Taj said, according to Iranian media.

In the statement carried by the state-run IRNA news agency, Taj said on Friday that Iran had presented conditions tied to participation, including guarantees over visas, security and treatment of Iranian players and officials, and added that the Islamic Republic would take part "without retreating from our beliefs, culture and convictions".

Iran is in a fragile ceasefire with the United States after the US and Israel sparked a war with attacks on Iran on February 28.

Iran war live updates: For the latest news on the Middle East crisis, read our blog.

Iranian citizens are currently subject to a travel ban imposed by the Trump administration.

The remarks came after Canadian authorities last month denied entry to Taj ahead of a FIFA Congress, reportedly because of his past ties to Iran's powerful Revolutionary Guard, which both the US and Canada have designated as a terrorist organisation.

Mehdi Taremi currently plays for Greek Super League side Olympiacos. (Getty Images: ANP/Bart Stoutjesdijk)

Taj has repeatedly said that Iran would seek assurances from FIFA that Iranian officials and players, and the national flag and anthem, would be treated with respect during the World Cup.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Concerns over issuing visas to people who had completed their mandatory military service in the Guard had been raised previously by others.

The matter potentially could affect one of Iran's key players, Mehdi Taremi, team captain and a striker who had completed his mandatory military service in the Guard.

In Iran, conscripts also can be assigned to the police or the army, often at random.

Iran's team has drawn with Belgium, New Zealand and Egypt in Group G and opens the World Cup against New Zealand in Inglewood, next to Los Angeles.

Iran has qualified for four consecutive World Cups and seven overall but has never advanced out of the group stage. Currently ranked number 21 in the world, Iran lost just one match in the Asian qualifying.

World.title: Singer Kira Puru was 'immediately humbled' on first acting job
World.content:
When Kira Puru (she/they) shared their last single following a year-long hiatus from releasing music, they thanked listeners for sticking by them.

"Your support really means the world to me right now," the Melbourne-based, Māori singer-songwriter wrote in an Instagram post announcing All My Boyfriends back in 2023.

Heaped in 00s nostalgia with an irresistible hook and soul-baring lyrics, the track exemplified everything Puru had developed a reputation for over a decade in the industry, with career highlights including a number-one hit on the triple j chart, a Hottest 100 spot and collaborations with the likes of Paul Kelly.

Loading Instagram content

From the outside, things seemed to be looking up following the COVID pandemic.

Then Puru went dark again.

In the almost three years since All My Boyfriends came out, she hasn't released any music. She also took a break from performing live, instead leaning into photography, graphic design and creative direction.

This year marks their return to the limelight — albeit, not in the way their followers might have anticipated.

In lieu of dropping new tracks, Puru appears alongside some of Australia's biggest stars in two comedy series.

First came a spot in dark comedy crime mystery hit Deadloch, followed by a role in new arts industry satire Bad Company.

Stream Bad Company now on ABC iview Margie, the unstable artistic director of the iconic theatre company, The Argyle, is up for the fight of her life, when Julia is hi-jacked from her corporate career to save the place from financial ruin.

In the latter, they play Kat, the first point of call at a theatre on the brink of collapse after years of being run into the ground by its nepotistic, spendthrift of an artistic director Margie (series creator and star Anne Edmonds).

Kat, Margie and the rest of The Argyle Theatre crew must find a way to work with the new girlboss chief executive Julia (Kitty Flanagan), hired by the board to save the institution from financial ruin.

Puru brings an understated humour to the role that feels so expertly crafted it's hard to believe this is only their second ever acting gig.

But what's behind the career pivot?

We caught up with Puru to find this out — and whether we can expect to hear new music from them on the airwaves anytime soon.

Have you always wanted to act?

I've always been a bit of a theatrical person — probably to the dismay of my parents, I imagine.

I did a little bit of acting when I was a teenager. Without giving my full age away, it's been a pretty long break between then and now.

But acting doesn't feel totally foreign to my experience as a musician.

Puru also resumed playing live shows again in the last few months, which they had "really missed ... it feels amazing." (Supplied)

Making music videos and stuff, there's a lot of performance, and there's a lot of acting involved in singing on stage.

I've definitely done gigs when I have not felt like being perceived by hundreds of thousands of people.

So how did the roles in Deadloch and Bad Company come about?

It kind of all happened by accident. I got an audition request for Deadloch — I indirectly know the Kates [series creators Kate McLennan and Kate McCartney] and I've been a massive fan for a long time.

I vaguely remember [tweeting at them], "Please put me in something", before I deleted my Twitter.

So, that role could just have been manifestation, to a degree. [Laughs]

Puru nabbed the role of musician Flora in Deadloch after sending in her first ever self-tape (pictured). (Supplied)

I was extremely nervous before the audition because I'd never done a self-tape before, but it felt like it would be something I might regret if I didn't do it.

And I lucked out! I did feel like I probably should have tried doing a little bit more acting before [appearing] on an internationally adored television show.

Loading Instagram content

I'd never even been on a TV set like that before … I didn't know what any of the lingo was. I didn't even know that you have to film the same scene 25 times ... I just thought, "This is going to be easy. How hard could it be? Acting is so chill."

I was humbled pretty immediately after arriving on set. But I feel so lucky to be involved, and everyone was very kind and patient.

I almost didn't do the audition that landed me the part for Bad Company, because it was in-person. Of course, I hadn't done that before either, and I was s****ing myself.

But I challenged myself to do it even though I was terrified and that one went really great, too.

The audition was actually for a different production that had something to do with the queen. I didn't get that part, but somebody passed my [tape] along to the [Bad Company] casting agent … that might have been the way it went.

As you can tell, I'm obviously not paying full attention to what's going on around me at all times [laughs]. I'm just happy to be here.

Puru says Anne Edmonds told them Kat served "the role of the audience" in Bad Company, as "one of the more normal people at The Argyle". (ABC/Guesswork Television: Sarah Enticknap)

What are you trying to say through your art at the moment?

I didn't really plan for a career pivot, but eventually, around COVID time, things just started to get a lot more difficult.

I left the label I was signed to, as well as my manager.

COVID meant I couldn't perform live in the way I was used to and coming back after all of the lockdowns, my career just wasn't the same — it was much harder to fill rooms and sell tickets.

Loading Instagram content

I spent a couple of years trying to push that but it felt really difficult. I was feeling pretty burnt out, and I needed to take a break.

My goal since then has been about making art because I like it and it feels good. More about whether the process of performing a song is joyful to me, and less about career accolades or travel or getting a number-one hit.

I just started playing shows again in the last six months after a couple of years off, and that felt really amazing. I'd missed it.

So yeah, I don't know right now. I'm just enjoying new experiences and making art for the sake of it, and trying to forget about clout and money and profile.

I also have the luxury now of a few different outlets, which is nice.

Kira the multi-hyphenate!

I guess … I feel like the most annoying people in the arts use that term, though. I will use it from time to time. But I feel like it's annoying. [Laughs]

Do you have plans to release any music in the near future?

There's new music being made. And I've got a lot of fun little projects with friends … I would love to be releasing music again soon, but I'm waiting for a sign from the universe, basically.

I don't know if it's a little "woo woo" or whatever, but I would love to feel wholly that it's time and that it's right before I do it, because the experience of doing it before was so hard and I just don't think something that's brought me so much joy in my life should feel so difficult.

For now, Puru is "enjoying new experiences and making art for the sake of it". (ABC/Guesswork Television: Sarah Enticknap)

What's coming up for you in the acting space?

I just did my third ever audition in the last couple weeks, so hopefully I'll get a call back. But what I've learned recently is that you don't always hear when you get a part or not, which is kind of bananas.

But I had also started writing a television show with my friend even before Deadloch and Bad Company …

That's quite frankly huge news! Did you learn anything about making TV from Edmonds and Flanagan on set that stuck with you?

I've always admired Eddo and her comedy so much, she really makes me laugh. I think she's f***ing bananas and her instincts are just unbridled … She keeps you on your toes and she's really fearless and free, which I appreciate a lot.

The project that inspired Anne Edmonds' satire of the arts world Everything Anne Edmonds has done over the last two decades has been leading to Bad Company.

And Kitty is … I wouldn't say the total opposite; she can have a really unhinged, dark sense of humour. But she's a lot more prepared and intentional in the way she performs. Between takes she'll just go totally silent and be doing her lines, she's so collected and composed.

Having those two people on set everyday was super valuable, because it gave me the whole spectrum of how you could approach the work.

That seems to align pretty closely with their characters in the show. Who would you rather have as a boss — Margie or Julia?

Oh, Margie, 100 per cent. 20 minutes of clapping in the morning and saying "Eh oh! Eh oh!" is gonna be far better than whatever Julia's got me doing.

I think every normal person would prefer to be doing some icebreaker activity than, I don't know, running the numbers. But maybe I'm not normal, actually.

I don't think I know anyone who'd want to go around in a circle first thing and talk about themselves. But morning clapping, sure.

Actually you're right, you're right. Maybe I'd like to take it on a day-by-day basis.

Sometimes I'm a Margie girl, other days I'm a Julia type, you know?

The last day on set for Bad Company. (Supplied)

What was the weirdest thing that happened on set beyond the 'Eh oh! Eh ohs'?

There was a day where we spent about half an hour with Eddo rubbing my fringe against my forehead, which was interesting.

They did have an intimacy coordinator call me to ask if that would be OK, so it was all aboveboard. And I was like, "Yeah, so long as she doesn't pull any hair out of my head, I'm fine."

At first I thought it was kind of wild that an intimacy coordinator was pulled in for that, but actually I think it speaks to the production and how much they cared about us all.

The Argyle Theatre's marketing strategy pretty much boils down to 'copious totes'. Are you for or against the copious totes?

I have too many totes myself, I need to pass on a few. So, I can't totally s**t on copious totes.

The "copious totes" in question. (ABC/Guesswork Television: Sarah Enticknap)

From an environmental standpoint, I think the world has enough totes. But what else would the performative male use to carry his bell hooks book and his reusable coffee cup, if he didn't have a local theatre tote bag?

So ultimately, yes to the totes?

[Laughs]. I'm gonna say, "Sure".

Quotes lightly edited for clarity and brevity.

Watch Bad Company free on ABC iview and on Sundays at 8:15pm on ABC TV.

World.title: Live: Iran's IRGC threatens US sites as Trump awaits Tehran response
World.content:
Qatari LNG tanker Al Kharaitiyat has sailed towards the Strait of Hormuz after departing Qatar's Ras Laffan, according to LSEG shipping data.

The ship is reportedly en route to Port Qasim in Pakistan.

Sources have told Reuters the move was approved by Iran to build confidence with Qatar and Pakistan, both mediators in the war.

Pakistan has been in discussions with Iranto allow a limited number of LNG tankers to pass through the strait, as Islamabad urgently needs to address its gas shortage, a source briefed on the agreement told Reuters.

There was no immediate comment from QatarEnergy.

If completed, it would mark the first transit of a Qatari LNG vessel through the strait since the conflict started.

World.title: How a post office in a train carriage became a popular meeting spot
World.content:
When the town's post office and general store announced it would be closing at short notice eight years ago, Clackline residents had one month to come up with a solution before services ceased.

The Wheatbelt town, 80km east of Perth, is home to just 330 people.

A small group of volunteers banded together to come up with a solution — transforming a vacant train carriage into a fully operational post office.

The former sleeper train carriage was transformed into the Clackline Post office in 2018. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Eliza Bidstrup)

Former Clackline Progress Association president Michael Letch called a community meeting to discuss the issue in 2018, unsure if anyone would attend.

"When [my wife and I] rolled up to the meeting, we couldn't find a parking spot because there were 70 people there," he said.

Former Clackline Progress Association president Michael Letch spearheaded the post office relocation. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Eliza Bidstrup)

"I don't think anyone took any notice of the unusual idea of the post office being in the carriage, as long as it was going to stay in Clackline.

"The whole community came together over that month to bring the idea to life."

Sleeper car transformed

Trains moved through Clackline to Northam and Toodyay until 1966, when a new rail route was opened.

Until its renovation, the carriage sat vacant on land across the road from the former general store.

The Clackline Post Office is a former sleeper train carriage that travelled through the town. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Eliza Bidstrup)

Mr Letch said the new use of the train was fitting.

"The carriage was a sleeper car on the Kalgoorlie Express, and it used to thunder through Clackline," he said.

"In the earlier days, the to-ing and fro-ing of mail was by rail."

Community hub

Eight years on, the post office has become a community hub that includes a library and gardens, hosting daily catch-ups between locals.

The community garden at the Clackline Post Office was established by the late postmaster Laurie O'Neil. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Eliza Bidstrup)

"With the loss of the school many years ago and the store, this has become a community centre," he said.

Clackline Post Office postmaster Carol O'Neil has been running the post office since the day it opened, motivated by the encouragement of her late husband, Laurie.

Mrs O'Neil said the connection the post office provided the community was vital, given its small population.

Clackline Post Office postmaster Carol O'Neil has worked in the carriage since its inception. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Eliza Bidstrup)

"We get mums who catch up out the front on their way home from dropping the kids off at the bus stop, people who are new to the town who get to be a part of something," she said.

"Before the post office was here, people would say hello in the street, but they didn't get the chance to know each other."

World.title: Cider mill makes sweet comeback after 100 years
World.content:
When Braidwood carpenter Ned Bott was asked to refurbish a cider mill built by the Albert Day Foundry in Somerset in 1868, he had to do some serious guesswork about what the original looked like.

There are no simple instruction manuals online for such an old piece of machinery.

"We spent hours trying to find images of a similar type of mill, but to no avail," he said.

"So I had to work off what was there and recreate what I believed to be in existence at the time.

" Apart from the main timber frame, I had to rebuild all the timber parts and the hopper, the catch box, steel-toothed rollers, the roller box, and remade a few forged components, and wire-brushed for days trying to clean up the iron. "

Loading...

But with the old mill restored, he finally had a breakthrough that will allow him to put the finishing touches on it.

"In the last couple of weeks, we managed to get hold of someone who posted some photos of the same mill on a farm in Hestercombe [UK]. We got to find out a few more intricate parts we were missing, so there's a little bit more work to do on this," Mr Bott said.

First crush delights crowd

The cider mill had its first apple crush in more than 100 years on the weekend as part of a demonstration at the Braidwood Museum and Heritage Centre.

Not only did it perform well, but there are plans to use it regularly.

"I've reproduced this to be functional, and not just a museum piece," Mr Bott said.

"We'll use it next year, and I'll hopefully get the job to fix an apple press from the early 1900s, which is capable of pressing one tonne or more at any time, so if we get this going too, it'll be quite a sight."

Braidwood cider maker Gary Sully wants to use the cider mill to crush apples grafted from its original property. (ABC News: Floss Adams)

There are also plans to produce cider using apples grown on the very property where the mill was kept at Majors Creek, south of Braidwood.

"Many years ago, we grafted the root remnant trees of the Wilton Cider Factory, where the press and presser came from," Braidwood cider maker Gary Sully said.

" My dream is to get enough apples off the trees we've grafted and create the same cider they made in that day, using the same equipment. "

Mill was once breakthrough technology

The original Albert Day mill, pictured prior to its significant refurbishment. (Supplied: Gary Sully)

Mr Sully said this style of mill, known as an Ingenio mill, revolutionised cider-making when it was invented in the 1670s.

"Originally, the mills would've been stone troughs with a big stone wheel drawn around by a horse that crushed everything, including pips and stalks.

"This Ingenio mill was a watershed moment in cider making because it allowed a gap for the pips and stalks to go through the roller.

"Pips are full of arsenic, so they'll impart a bitter taste, and you get a rougher, unrefined drink."

Major refurbishment takes time

Mr Bott said it was about four weeks' worth of work, completed over the space of one and a half years.

The carpenter is used to being resourceful when it comes to machinery.

Ned Bott got interested in beer brewing during COVID lockdown and then switched to cider. (Supplied: Gary Sully)

During the COVID lockdown, he built his own cider mill using objects he found around his house and started making his own drinks.

"We'd collect apples from trees on the side of the road, and I'd get a workforce together and help make cider," he said.

"Then I got word there was an apple chitter at the museum that needed fixing up, and I was more than happy to take on the project."

World.title: Ongoing breakdowns hamper breast screening service in Tasmania
World.content:
Angie Bisset had a mammogram booked on what is currently Tasmania's only mobile breast screening bus.

But the night before her long-awaited appointment, she received a call informing her the bus had "broken down" and would not be coming to Smithton in Tasmania's far north-west, where Ms Bisset lives.

She was given the option to re-book for June, which she took, conscious of the risks that could arise from delayed detection.

Angie Bisset says she is "close to the age" when her mum became sick. (Supplied: Angie Bisset)

Ms Bisset's mother died from breast cancer at age 43, something that weighs on her mind with every passing year.

"The fact that I'm close to the age when she got sick scares me so much," she said.

A young Angie Bisset (left) with her mother before she died of breast cancer. (Supplied: Angie Bisset)

Last year, Ms Bisset was not able to access the bus and had to travel from Smithton to Launceston — a 460-kilometre round trip — to have her mammogram, something she's not keen to do again amid rising fuel prices.

"I'm worried if this gets cancelled again, then I'm going to have no choice but to travel three hours just to get the scan done," she said.

" If I could, I would go private, but … I can't afford anything like that at the moment. "

Angie Bisset (right) and her mother (left). (Supplied: Angie Bisset)

Both BreastScreen buses affected by technical issues

The BreastScreen bus Luna, which serviced the state's south and the east coast, was taken off the road after water damage and technical issues caused two staff to receive electric shocks.

At the time, the Department of Health acknowledged "any reduction in screening rates increases the risk of women being diagnosed with breast cancer at later stages, when the cancer is more difficult and expensive to treat".

One of the Breastscreen units pictured in 2025. (Supplied: Kristie Johnston)

At the end of April, mammography equipment on BreastScreen Tasmania's bus Ida malfunctioned.

While the issue has been resolved and services have resumed, women like Ms Bisset, who have had to reschedule their appointments, have been left feeling anxious about the delays.

Leanne Roberson believes a BreastScreen Tasmania check saved her life. (Supplied: Leanne Roberson)

A potentially life-saving service

Leanne Roberson was 57 when the BreastScreen Tasmania bus made a stop in her hometown, which she believes saved her life.

"It was the last appointment of the day, and I hesitantly went because it was a cold, miserable day.

" I'm so glad I did, though, because … if I had waited 12 months, it might have been too late for me. "

Leanne Roberson is grateful to still be here to enjoy time with her family. (Supplied: Leanne Roberson)

The Ulverstone woman was diagnosed with stage 2 breast cancer and was able to have the tumour removed while retaining her breast.

When she learned about the situation at Smithton through a Facebook post, she felt compelled to share her own story, which was met with an overwhelmingly positive response.

"People want to have these checks done, and they can't access them," she said.

" I am so thankful to BreastScreen for catching my cancer early and allowing me to be here with my beautiful family and grandson. "

Labor's Anita Dow is calling on the government to improve access for regional women to BreastScreen services. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Braddon Labor MP Anita Dow said delays in accessing BreastScreen services showed the health of Tasmanian women in regional and remote communities was not being prioritised.

Ms Dow said the government had been slow to deliver its commitment to improving access to BreastScreen services.

"These are really important issues for regional Tasmanians who have to travel long distances to access specialist services and, quite rightly, they deserve commitments that have been made by the government to be delivered in a timely fashion," she said in parliament on Wednesday.

" Surely … access to BreastScreen services isn't too much to ask. "

Premier Jeremy Rockliff said "accessibility to women's health services is very important to me, it's very important to our team, and it's very important we get it right".

In a statement, a Department of Health spokesperson confirmed the screening equipment on board Ida "experienced technical issues, requiring replacement parts to be ordered from overseas as a priority".

Jeremy Rockliff says an effective breast screening service for women is "very important to me". (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

The issue has now been resolved, with Ida set to return to Smithton from May 18 to 22, then again from June 9 to 19 this year, they said.

"Clients who had their appointments postponed have had the opportunity to re-book when the unit returns. New clients are also being contacted to fill future appointment availabilities," the spokesperson said.

The new Devonport BreastScreen clinic is scheduled to open next month, and the department spokesperson said the delivery of a new mobile screening unit is "on track for completion later this year, with design and planning completed and construction to commence shortly".

The spokesperson said these projects, as well as the new Tasmanian Breast Care Centre at the Royal Hobart Hospital opening this month, will "provide a significant increase in access to breast screening for Tasmanian women".

The BreastScreen Tasmania Client Travel Subsidy is available to ensure Tasmanians can access breast screening services, as well as other community transport arrangements, the spokesperson said.

" BreastScreen Tasmania also helps to resolve any barriers for clients in accessing this important service at an individual level. "

World.title: WA teens say anonymous 'alt' accounts used to bypass social media ban
World.content:
Teenagers in Western Australia's north are warning there are multiple ways to circumvent Australia's world-first social media ban for under-16s amid concerns about accounts spreading malicious content.

Methods include creating anonymous or fake profiles, also known as "alt" accounts.

The comments come after a Broome student was assaulted after mistakenly being thought responsible for a fake account.

Shirley Wynne says reported posts and comments can take weeks to be removed from social media platforms. (ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson)

Broome Senior High School student Shirley Wynne said young people were hiding behind these accounts to post gossip and malicious content.

The 15-year-old said reporting within the platforms was not a quick fix, and comments or posts could take weeks to be removed after being flagged.

"It varies, but a lot slides," she said.

"It's hard to get something taken down … it's very like unlikely for your report to actually work."

Kyra Herveux says young people are not always using social media for the right reasons. (ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson)

Kyra Herveux, who attends St Mary's College in Broome, said many people were not using social media correctly.

"They create fake accounts, spread gossip and are really mean to other people," she said.

Bullying escalates

In April, a student spent more than 24 hours in hospital after being assaulted during an incident at Broome Senior High School.

Her mother, who the ABC has chosen not to name, said her daughter was kicked repeatedly by another student and sustained a broken tooth.

The student sustained a broken tooth during the incident at Broome Senior High School. (Supplied)

Prior to the incident, the mother said other students had made a fake account depicting her daughter.

She said social media had a "big impact" on young people, and increased awareness was needed to address violence in schools.

"They're still kids … they don't know how bad this can be, or how much they can hurt someone else," she said.

The assault took place between students after school at Broome Senior High School. (ABC Kimberley: Sam Tomlin)

The mother said school staff had been doing "everything they could" to ensure her daughter felt safe to return to school.

'Clear consequences'

In a statement, the WA Department of Education said it was aware of the incident, and violence was taken "extremely seriously".

"There are clear and immediate consequences for students who engage in anti-social behaviour," a spokesperson said.

They said while principals and teachers had access to the resources to "take firm action", the issue was not something schools could tackle alone.

"Parents, caregivers, families and the wider community all have a role to play in reinforcing respect and appropriate behaviour," they said.

A WA police spokesperson said investigations were continuing into the incident.

Calls for more education

It has been about six months since the national ban came into effect, and students in Broome agreed not much had changed.

Lily Malcolm says reported posts and comments on TikTok can take weeks to be removed from the platform. (ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson)

Broome Senior High School student Lily Malcolm said there should be better education about social media, instead of "just taking it away".

"They didn't try to fix social media problems, they just banned it," she said.

The 14-year-old said there needed to be better regulations ensuring flagged content was removed.

"The reports actually working and getting through, if they're [young people] getting bullied and feel unsafe," Lily said.

In a statement, an eSafety spokesperson said they were aware some teens continued to access social media accounts and "reasonable steps" were being taken to prevent this.

"We are working directly with social media companies to strengthen and uplift safety practices, and there will continue to be noticeable changes in underage detection and locking of accounts, as well as other compliance improvements," they said.

" Where companies fail to address these safety shortcomings, formal regulatory investigations and enforcement action will be forthcoming. "

World.title: China can’t get enough of the world’s stinkiest fruit. Now, fresh meat is coming to Australia
World.content:
WorldAsiaFood China can’t get enough of the world’s stinkiest fruit. Now, fresh meat is coming to Australia Zach Hope May 10, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Penang/Kuala Lumpur: The durian, aka the “king of fruits”, is not for everyone. Gordon Chong says when his mates sliced up samples at a pop-up shop in Melbourne’s The Glen shopping centre last year, a concerned citizen, sniffing something awry, phoned Triple 0 to report a gas leak. The Glen didn’t confirm specifics*, but it would not be especially unusual. The inimitable fruit’s record of waft “emergencies” in Australia includes evacuations of universities, libraries and hospitals. Gordon Chong and Jerry Fong are bringing fresh durian to Australia on overnight flights from Malaysia. Ruby Alexander In 2003, a Virgin Blue flight from Brisbane to Adelaide was delayed four hours as cargo handlers investigated the source of what chief executive Brett Godfrey said was “just the most pungent, disgusting smell”. “This wasn’t a safety issue, this was a gross issue,” he said after the offender – durian stowed in a passenger’s luggage – was found and cleared. “No one wants to fly in an aeroplane that smells like that.”



Evidently, Godfrey is not a fan. Western palettes and noses are not accustomed to such joys. “An Aussie walks past and will be like, ‘gas leak’,” says Chong, a Malaysian who moved to Australia 25 years ago. “An Asian walks past and says, ‘Durian! I’m buying it’.” Chong says he had to fly home to get his pungent, sweet, custardy fix. Then, a few years ago, frozen Malaysian durian pulp started appearing in Asian groceries. It was “pretty nice” but not the real deal. Premium Malaysian durian with a view at Penang’s Durian Tree House. That’s musang king on the right. Zach Hope Certain Coles and Woolworths stores now occasionally stock the whole fruit. The problem is, they also arrive frozen. More offensive to Malay sensibilities is that they are an imported variety from Thailand, and “actually horrible”.



Chong and friend Jerry Fong agreed something must be done, so they set up Durian Lah, a side gig that puts them at the experimental edge of Australia’s minuscule durian game. “We don’t want to do frozen because you can buy it from anywhere,” Chong says. “We want the fresh ones. That’s what people are craving.” The business is so new it hasn’t even received its first shipment (durian season is just starting in Malaysia), but the idea is to fly in fresh durian pulp on overnight flights from Kuala Lumpur to Melbourne. Durians have an exceedingly short – and sensitive – shelf life, so customers must then make haste to Durian Lah warehouses in Vermont and Preston to collect their orders. “We’re just waiting for the arrival date and the price, and off we go,” Chong says.



The first run of 400g packs might retail for $50 to $70 each, dropping in price later in the year as more fruit comes online in Malaysia. People are willing to pay, he says, because “it’s just that childhood taste that you can’t get”. “People who know durian, they know.” Simon Chua collecting freshly dropped durians from his netting. Zach Hope Chong’s passion is a glimpse of durian devotion embedded through swathes of South-East Asia. In Malaysia, the fruiting season activates family gatherings and spawns ubiquitous street sellers. In Singapore, members of parliament – yes, politicians – lead constituents on sold-out tours over the border to feast on all-you-can-eat durian buffets. Durian etiquette in Asia holds that it must be consumed out of nose-shot of the public. Signs on buses, trains and hotel elevators ram home the point.



For full disclosure, I love durian. It is nutty, buttery, sweet and filling. My wife, however, is more of the Brett Godfrey mind. She bought an orange ice-cream once, believing it was mango-flavoured, and realised quick smart she should have had a closer look. The durian ice cream went into an outside bin, and the taste from just one lick, she insisted on reminding me, lingered into the evening. There remains a total durian ban in our household. Loading So, my trip to the Durian Tree House in Penang recently was a joy. It is run by husband and wife team Simon Chua and Yvonne Tan on about 30 acres of mountainous terrain overlooking the Strait of Malacca.



Some of the towering trees on their property are more than 60 years old: the older the tree, the better the fruit. Part of the business is accommodation. They also open up tables for the day-trippers – like a durian cellar door. To serve, Chua first bashes the hard outer casing with the flat side of his machete to trigger the “fermentation” he says makes for creamier, richer flesh. The idea is to gorge with friends, starting from the less prestigious varieties and working your way up to the black thorn and musang king (known in China as the “Hermès” of durian), savouring the changing flavours and textures from one fruit to the next. “Human, you take care of – baby, take care, take care, and they grow up with the good qualities, very smart. The tree has a life too,” Chua says.



“You need to use a lot of fertiliser, you need to water, you need to care. Sometimes you need to also sing a song.” Come again? A customer might be waiting for a specific number of durians and singing, Chua explains, smooths the farmer-tree collaboration. ‘Chinese people visit Malaysia and they try durian and love it. And when Chinese people love something, it just, you know, goes viral.’ Gordon Chong He offers one of his ditties, translating from the Chinese for my benefit: “Black thorn, black thorn, give me a few. I need you to drop from tree.” Not so long ago, durian farming in Malaysia was just a hobby, or grown professionally, but for local consumption only.



These days, the industry, centred in Thailand (the biggest exporter), Vietnam, Indonesia and Malaysia, has ballooned into a multibillion-dollar behemoth, turning battling farmers into fruit moguls. ‘The durian index’ Like many profound transformations, it is because of China. From a few hundred million dollars worth of durian product a decade ago, China, now in the midst of a durian craze, last year imported a staggering US$7.5 billion ($10.4 billion). This is more than a third of the country’s total intake of foreign fruit in terms of dollar value. Chong, in Melbourne, puts it this way: “Because of tourism, Chinese people visit Malaysia and they try durian and love it. And when Chinese people love something, it just, you know, goes viral.”



Some have proposed a “durian index”, arguing that patterns of Chinese consumption may provide reliable early indicators about the state of the country’s broader economy. Thai and Vietnamese farmers have the inside running with the Chinese masses because of their geographical proximity – cheaper freight means cheaper, fresher durians. Chinese tourists tucking in at the Durian Tree House. They plan to tick off five different varieties. Zach Hope But Malaysians tend to turn up their noses at the Thai varieties. Chong, being diplomatic, describes the subdued taste of the Thai fruit as like a pinot noir to Malaysian musang king’s full-bodied shiraz. Malaysian varieties, symbols of wealth and discernment in China, have a diplomatic function, too. In 2024, Malaysia’s king Ibrahim gave Chinese President Xi Jinping two boxes of the good stuff during a state visit. Malaysia’s prime minister Anwar Ibrahim and Chinese Premier Li Qiang also scoffed musang king and black thorn earlier the same year.



Purists will crack a durian and pull the sweet, soft flesh straight from the spiky casing with their bare fingers. But for milder experiences, try durian ice cream, cakes or confectionery. Dr Tan Sue Yee, chief executive of Top Fruits, one of Malaysia’s biggest exporters, says you can turn durian into about 90 products, even spaghetti. Dr Tan Sue Yee at his Kuala Lumpur headquarters. Zach Hope “For the past four or five years, the whole market has been moving – growth is 20-30 per cent each year,” he says. “That’s until last season – it became a durian tsunami.” He is referring to the perfect growing conditions that created a glut, forcing down prices. Oversupply has been exacerbated by new farms: trees planted a decade ago, at the beginning of Chinese interest, are now bearing their first batches of good fruit.



Tan, though, is not worried. Lower prices mean lower expectations, which can be a good thing, he says. In any case, he projects the value of the entire South-East Asian durian industry to more than double over the next six years to about US$45 billion. There is room for everyone. “The next target is India,” he says. “Ohhh, the Indian market will be very good.” Dr Tan’s durian pizza is bestseller in China. Zach Hope An assistant brings in the company’s top seller: a pizza covered in cheese and golf ball-sized globs of durian. I wouldn’t reach for it again. The Chinese, however, buy as many as 300,000 of them a month. “We do a stinking business,” Tan quips.



He jokes that I, as a durian man, could be his pizza agent in Australia. I explain that we are not ready. Australians need to settle the pineapple debate before introducing, of all things, the stinkiest fruit in the world. *A spokesperson for The Glen shopping centre says: “There have been occasions when the centre management team received calls from customers concerned about a possible gas leak due to a noticeable smell.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: National News Live: One Nation win in historic victory as Liberal Party lose regional NSW seat for first time in 77 years
World.content:
Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson says last night’s vote is a “serious situation” for his party.

The Liberals won 12.4 per cent of the primary vote in the Farrer byelection, which Wilson said could partly be blamed on the Nationals running a candidate in the electorate for the first time in almost 25 years.

Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson. Dominic Lorrimer

“Which is not to downplay it. It is a serious situation, but what it reflects is the need for us to be bigger, better, bolder, confident Liberals defining the future of the country,” he told the ABC’s Insiders.

Asked how last night’s vote should reflect on Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, Wilson said: “It shows that there’s a lot of work we’ve got to do, and Angus has been very upfront about that.”

Wilson said Labor should also take a lesson from the Liberal wipeout.

“One of the most consistent messages [from Farrer was] people want somebody who’s going to fight for them and for their future … and people are going to be very antagonistic towards the government breaking promises on tax issues.”

World.title: Europe out, Maldives in: How the Iran war is affecting tour operators
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesTourism Europe out, Maldives in: How the Iran war is affecting tour operators Chris Zappone May 10, 2026 — 8:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two months after the war in the Middle East sparked a wave of trip cancellations reminiscent of the COVID lockdowns, Australian travellers and tour operators are beginning to adapt by pivoting toward destinations outside of Europe and the embattled region. The outbreak of war in March punched a significant hole in tourism revenues as escalating tensions between Iran, Israel and the US left many travellers stranded or unable to depart. Tour operators now say the panic is subsiding as consumers seek out alternative itineraries but continue to travel. The Maldives are one of the destinations Australians are turning to as war affects the Middle East. Adobe Stock “The first few weeks were really tough, it almost reminded us of COVID a bit,” said Brett Mitchell, the Australian head of Intrepid Tours. “A lot of cancellations and people calling for advice: ‘Do I go? Do I not go?’” Slumps of 75 to 80 per cent in bookings in the first few weeks of the war were “pretty standard”, industry sources said, as travellers, tour operators and airlines grappled with the surprise closure of the Middle Eastern air corridor, thousands of flight cancellations and paralysing uncertainty.



The crisis raised questions about the future of holiday travel to the Middle East and Europe. But unlike the grounding of flights during the pandemic border closures, in March and April, as drones and missiles flew across the Persian Gulf, the local appetite for travel and tours remained strong. Something closer to come: A tour group in Milford Sound, New Zealand. Nine Mitchell said that the “vast majority” of customers who cancelled tours wanted credits for future Intrepid tours, not refunds. Today, there were a lot fewer cancellations for tours, he said, and customers were starting to come back and book. “We’re past those crisis days now, things are starting to stabilise,” Mitchell said. “People are still travelling, they are just changing where they want to go.” The freeze on activity in the Middle East is reflected in the drop in tourist travel through the region.



Just last year, 2.8 million Australians travelled to the United Arab Emirates, while 1.78 million travelled to Qatar, primarily as stopover points to Europe. This month, 35 per cent of take-off and landing slots across the 30 Middle Eastern airports, including in Dubai, Abu Dhabi, and Saudi Arabia, have been cancelled, according to slot managing company Airport Coordination Limited. Related Article Aviation Shall we go to Europe? Travellers bet both ways on flights during Iran war Customers who might have booked for Europe and blanched at a Middle East transfer are instead looking to South-East Asia and Japan. “We’re seeing a lot of the new bookings coming in now, mainly going closer to home,” Mitchell said. Demand for travel within Australia has jumped 20 per cent at Intrepid, he noted. The company was booking tours to the Northern Territory, the Kimberley in Western Australia and Cape York.



As for the future of tours in Europe and the Middle East, things are less clear. Destination Artisans caters to well-to-do couples and families with tailored, private tours of places in France and Belgium, but it doesn’t arrange their flights. “People are still travelling, they are just changing where they want to go,” says Intrepid Australia and NZ boss Brett Mitchell. Co-founder Norma Keshishian said her company was not “directly affected” by the Middle East conflict. “However, my total number of trips confirmed is much lower than last year.” “I think people are just spooked and not travelling; certainly bookings to France are down from last year.”



The government’s travel warning hangs over the industry too. The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade maintains a level four “Do not travel” warning for Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Qatar. Even for Australians willing to chance it, travel insurance typically won’t cover the stopover. Insurer Allianz notes that “if a traveller transits through, or stops over in, a country that is subject to a “Do Not Travel” warning from the Australian government (Smartraveller), cover may be limited for any claims that arise in connection with that country or events linked to that warning”. Quieter for tour groups here too. The Rozenhoedkaai canal, historic brick houses and the Belfry in Bruges medieval Old Town, Belgium. Getty Images/iStockphoto That’s even as the policy can remain in effect for other destinations in Europe or Singapore. The elevated uncertainty is enough to dissuade travellers from spending tens of thousands of dollars on booking a tour. Adam Schwab, co-founder and CEO of Luxury Escapes, said losses of up to 80 per cent in the first month for the tour operator industry were “pretty standard”.



Volumes for Luxury Escape’s travel package business and its online travel agency both fell dramatically in March, but have since recovered, he said. Related Article Lunch with The fast talker building a luxury travel empire But revenues for its tour business have been hit harder. They dropped as much as 80 per cent in March and were still down 50 per cent, Schwab said, with tours to places like Morocco and Egypt “significantly impacted”. “We’re definitely seeing a drop-off,” he said. Since the conflict began, some people who had already booked a tour were either going ahead despite the uncertainty, or postponing. And yet others were shopping for trips, but not booking.



Schwab said travellers were now pivoting to destinations like Bali, Fiji, Vietnam and the Maldives, while deferring larger-scale tours. The preference could be seen in data generated through the company’s websites. A jaunt to the Indian Ocean is an option for some Australians avoiding the Middle Eastern hubs. iStock “Middle Eastern products generally aren’t converting [selling] particularly well,” said Schwab. Consequently, they ranked lower on the offerings to customers. Meanwhile, Fiji has recorded its highest-ever March arrivals, 71,765 visitors, up 12 per cent from March 2025. Australians accounted for 43 per cent of the total, up 17 per cent from last year. In this climate, Luxury Escapes has high hopes for its launch of charter flights to the Maldives from May 18. The flights from Melbourne to the Maldives in the Indian Ocean allowed passengers to avoid flying through the Middle Eastern hubs of Qatar or the United Arab Emirates, and cut what would be a 20-hour journey to 10 hours, Schwab said.



Related Article Aviation Flights cancelled, routes change as war uncertainty, fuel price grows Any unsold tickets would be covered by the Melbourne-based tour operator – part of a deal that was years in the making. But how long the charter foray lasts depends on what happens to fuel costs. The fuel costs for the flights were hedged for the first six months, making pricing on the charters competitive, said Schwab. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. World.title: Rock fisherman dies at dangerous headland on Central Coast
World.content:
NationalNSWTragedy Rock fisherman dies at dangerous headland on Central Coast Angus Dalton May 10, 2026 — 7:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man has died after a wave swept him into the ocean while rock fishing on a notoriously dangerous part of the Central Coast, between Sydney and Newcastle. Rescuers were called to Frazer Park within the Munmorah State Conservation Area about 1.20pm on Saturday after reports a fisherman had been swept into the surf. Snapper Point is a notoriously dangerous headland. Nine Three friends had been fishing off Snapper Point, north of Frazer Park beach and near a secluded campground. Two of the men were fishing off a higher platform when the third, a 41-year-old man, was knocked off a lower platform by a wave.



The man was wearing a flotation device around his torso, but no life jacket, a police spokesperson said. He clung to an Esky to stay afloat. One of his friends entered the water to try to save him but was unsuccessful. He was picked up by a passing boat and taken to Swansea RSL Club, uninjured. After 10 to 15 minutes, the man had let go of the Esky and was seen floating face-up in the surf, the spokesperson said. A paramedic on the Westpac Rescue helicopter winched down and retrieved the man’s body. The paramedics attempted CPR, but he could not be saved.



Police, Marine Area Command and Surf Life Saving NSW also took part in rescue efforts. Police are continuing to investigate the incident and preparing a report for the coroner. Related Article Tragedy The phone rang at 5.40pm. It became ‘the darkest night’ in these marine rescuers’ history Surf Life Saving NSW has described the area as notoriously dangerous, with “lots of rock crevasses and lots of caves”. More than 20 people have died since 2008 along the three-kilometre stretch of coastline where Snapper Point is located, including a rock fisher in 2019 who was swept off the point and into a treacherous sea cave. Several other people have drowned or been rescued after waves swept them from the rocks of Snapper Point. The jagged volcanic rock platforms on the point are popular with fishers.



Two rock fishers drowned at Little Beach in Bouddi National Park, also on the Central Coast, in March. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: This cancer is rising in young people like Nathan. There are ‘exquisite’ reasons not to despair
World.content:
Exclusive NationalCancer This cancer is rising in young people like Nathan. There are ‘exquisite’ reasons not to despair Kate Aubusson May 10, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nathan Borg was still groggy from anaesthesia when his doctor told him he had bowel cancer. The 29-year-old was three months shy of his wedding date. His fiancée, Samantha, sat next to him, sobbing. Nathan Borg was about to get married when he received his cancer diagnosis. Wolter Peeters “I had just bought a house, I had a mortgage, I was getting married,” Borg said. He assumed his colonoscopy would confirm the blood in his stool was due to haemorrhoids. “I never thought for a second that it was cancer.”



A growing number of young Australians are being diagnosed with bowel cancer for reasons that are not well understood. The incidence in people in their 30s is up 137 per cent since 2000. Related Article Exclusive

Prostate cancer It’s the deadliest cancer for Australian men. This test could be life-saving for many, and their daughters But a subset of patients – about one in six – seem to have tumours with a genomic quirk that makes them “exquisitely sensitive” to immunotherapies, as one global leader in precision oncology put it. An analysis of a cancer patient cohort whose tumours were considered incurable or advanced found that a third of bowel cancer patients were under 50 years of age. Almost 14 per cent of bowel cancer patients were under 40, the analysis of Omico’s database found. It’s an initiative that facilitates genomic profiling for cancer patients with poor prognoses and matches them with next-generation therapies or clinical trials.



Two per cent were aged under 30 (about 60 people). Fourteen patients were diagnosed with bowel cancer before they turned 25. “It is absolutely devastating to receive a diagnosis so young,” said David Thomas, the founder and chief scientist of Omico. Bowel cancer in young Australians is still very uncommon (the number of cases in 30- to 39-year-olds rose from a low base of 184 in the year 2000 to an estimated 772 in 2025, for example), and survival rates are rising. The vast majority of bowel cancers – also called colorectal cancer – are still among the over 50s (at which age Australians automatically receive a bowel cancer screening kit, although it can be requested from 45). However, the cancer can no longer be considered one of older people, Thomas said.



“We need to understand why the incidence of early onset colorectal cancer is rising. Is it environmental or microplastics? Is it diet? It isn’t genetics alone, but there may be a genetic component,” he said. Related Article Explainer

Cancer Why is cancer so hard to cure? Thomas said that up to 15 per cent of colorectal cancers have a genomic signature called microsatellite instability (MSI), which occurs when DNA mismatch repair proteins cannot fix errors in short DNA sequences. Most occur spontaneously, rather than being inherited. “These tumours are exquisitely sensitive to immunotherapies,” Thomas said. Borg’s cancer was one of them. He didn’t know at the time he began a deeply confronting sequence of radiation and chemotherapy to shrink his six-centimetre-long tumour, and surgery to remove 30 centimetres of his bowel, living with a stoma for six months.



“I lost my hair twice, and I had all the other fun symptoms of chemo,” he said sardonically. Borg had just bought a house, had a mortgage to pay and was about to be married. He could not afford to take time off work as a project manager for a commercial fit-out company. But when cancer spots were found in his liver, his oncologist found the key to his survival. Fittingly, Dr Siobhan O’Neill was sitting in a session at the Australian Gastro-Intestinal Tumours conference, and she opened up Borg’s Omico test results. He was “MSI-high”. “I jumped in my seat. I thought: ‘Oh, my God, this is amazing news. He can have immunotherapy’,” O’Neill said.



MSI testing is a routine part of the pathology process for newly diagnosed bowel cancer. Borg’s specific gene mutation meant there was no way to detect his tumour’s MSI signature without genomic testing. Further genomic testing found Borg had Lynch syndrome, an inherited genetic condition that accounts for about 3 per cent of colorectal cancers with MSI. Nathan Borg’s gruelling treatment regimen had to work around his wedding to his partner, Samantha, three months after his bowel cancer diagnosis. Borg had no trouble tolerating the PBS-funded immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab for his two-year course. He has been cancer-free since January.



“It was a game-changer,” Borg said. He and Samantha are expecting their first child in August. “I always knew I’d beat it in the end,” he said. Quick facts: bowel cancer patients in Omico’s cohort Bowel cancer accounted for 11.5 per cent of 3024 people who have been referred for comprehensive genomic profiling and treatment matching.

34 per cent of the bowel cancer participants in Omico’s programs are under 50, compared with 23.5 per cent across all other cancers

Almost 80 per cent of bowel cancer patients got a matched treatment recommendation

One in five enrolled in a clinical trial or accessed a treatment they were matched to after undergoing genomic profiling Cancer Australia chief executive Professor Dorothy Keefe said that lowering the bowel cancer screening age would cost an enormous amount of money that could be better spent, cause harm to people who don’t have cancer and clog up waiting lists for colonoscopies, which would delay cancer diagnoses Keefe urged young people to see their GP if they notice blood in their stools, changes in bowel habits, or any changes in their health that don’t resolve, including pain, vomiting, unexplained weight loss, fatigue or low haemoglobin.



Cancer Australia has commissioned an evidence review of early onset cancer risk factors, while updated evidence-based guidelines reflect how young people present with cancer and what investigations and referrals to pursue. “We, as a medical profession, need to reframe our thinking about cancer presentation in young people as this becomes more common,” Keefe said. Cancer Australia and the National Health and Medical Research Council announced on Monday $15 million to help fund seven research projects on early onset cancer risk factors, tests and treatments. Three projects will focus on colorectal cancer. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

In Malaysia, the fruiting season activates family gatherings and spawns ubiquitous street sellers. In Singapore, members of parliament – yes, politicians – lead constituents on sold-out tours over the border to feast on all-you-can-eat durian buffets. Durian etiquette in Asia holds that it must be consumed out of nose-shot of the public. Signs on buses, trains and hotel elevators ram home the point.



For full disclosure, I love durian. It is nutty, buttery, sweet and filling. My wife, however, is more of the Brett Godfrey mind. She bought an orange ice-cream once, believing it was mango-flavoured, and realised quick smart she should have had a closer look. The durian ice cream went into an outside bin, and the taste from just one lick, she insisted on reminding me, lingered into the evening. There remains a total durian ban in our household. Loading So, my trip to the Durian Tree House in Penang recently was a joy. It is run by husband and wife team Simon Chua and Yvonne Tan on about 30 acres of mountainous terrain overlooking the Strait of Malacca.



Some of the towering trees on their property are more than 60 years old: the older the tree, the better the fruit. Part of the business is accommodation. They also open up tables for the day-trippers – like a durian cellar door. To serve, Chua first bashes the hard outer casing with the flat side of his machete to trigger the “fermentation” he says makes for creamier, richer flesh. The idea is to gorge with friends, starting from the less prestigious varieties and working your way up to the black thorn and musang king (known in China as the “Hermès” of durian), savouring the changing flavours and textures from one fruit to the next. “Human, you take care of – baby, take care, take care, and they grow up with the good qualities, very smart. The tree has a life too,” Chua says.



“You need to use a lot of fertiliser, you need to water, you need to care. Sometimes you need to also sing a song.” Come again? A customer might be waiting for a specific number of durians and singing, Chua explains, smooths the farmer-tree collaboration. ‘Chinese people visit Malaysia and they try durian and love it. And when Chinese people love something, it just, you know, goes viral.’ Gordon Chong He offers one of his ditties, translating from the Chinese for my benefit: “Black thorn, black thorn, give me a few. I need you to drop from tree.” Not so long ago, durian farming in Malaysia was just a hobby, or grown professionally, but for local consumption only.



These days, the industry, centred in Thailand (the biggest exporter), Vietnam, Indonesia and Malaysia, has ballooned into a multibillion-dollar behemoth, turning battling farmers into fruit moguls. ‘The durian index’ Like many profound transformations, it is because of China. From a few hundred million dollars worth of durian product a decade ago, China, now in the midst of a durian craze, last year imported a staggering US$7.5 billion ($10.4 billion). This is more than a third of the country’s total intake of foreign fruit in terms of dollar value. Chong, in Melbourne, puts it this way: “Because of tourism, Chinese people visit Malaysia and they try durian and love it. And when Chinese people love something, it just, you know, goes viral.”



Some have proposed a “durian index”, arguing that patterns of Chinese consumption may provide reliable early indicators about the state of the country’s broader economy. Thai and Vietnamese farmers have the inside running with the Chinese masses because of their geographical proximity – cheaper freight means cheaper, fresher durians. Chinese tourists tucking in at the Durian Tree House. They plan to tick off five different varieties. Zach Hope But Malaysians tend to turn up their noses at the Thai varieties. Chong, being diplomatic, describes the subdued taste of the Thai fruit as like a pinot noir to Malaysian musang king’s full-bodied shiraz. Malaysian varieties, symbols of wealth and discernment in China, have a diplomatic function, too. In 2024, Malaysia’s king Ibrahim gave Chinese President Xi Jinping two boxes of the good stuff during a state visit. Malaysia’s prime minister Anwar Ibrahim and Chinese Premier Li Qiang also scoffed musang king and black thorn earlier the same year.



Purists will crack a durian and pull the sweet, soft flesh straight from the spiky casing with their bare fingers. But for milder experiences, try durian ice cream, cakes or confectionery. Dr Tan Sue Yee, chief executive of Top Fruits, one of Malaysia’s biggest exporters, says you can turn durian into about 90 products, even spaghetti. Dr Tan Sue Yee at his Kuala Lumpur headquarters. Zach Hope “For the past four or five years, the whole market has been moving – growth is 20-30 per cent each year,” he says. “That’s until last season – it became a durian tsunami.” He is referring to the perfect growing conditions that created a glut, forcing down prices. Oversupply has been exacerbated by new farms: trees planted a decade ago, at the beginning of Chinese interest, are now bearing their first batches of good fruit.



Tan, though, is not worried. Lower prices mean lower expectations, which can be a good thing, he says. In any case, he projects the value of the entire South-East Asian durian industry to more than double over the next six years to about US$45 billion. There is room for everyone. “The next target is India,” he says. “Ohhh, the Indian market will be very good.” Dr Tan’s durian pizza is bestseller in China. Zach Hope An assistant brings in the company’s top seller: a pizza covered in cheese and golf ball-sized globs of durian. I wouldn’t reach for it again. The Chinese, however, buy as many as 300,000 of them a month. “We do a stinking business,” Tan quips.



He jokes that I, as a durian man, could be his pizza agent in Australia. I explain that we are not ready. Australians need to settle the pineapple debate before introducing, of all things, the stinkiest fruit in the world. *A spokesperson for The Glen shopping centre says: “There have been occasions when the centre management team received calls from customers concerned about a possible gas leak due to a noticeable smell.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: National News Live: One Nation win in historic victory as Liberal Party lose regional NSW seat for first time in 77 years
World.content:
Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson says last night’s vote is a “serious situation” for his party.

The Liberals won 12.4 per cent of the primary vote in the Farrer byelection, which Wilson said could partly be blamed on the Nationals running a candidate in the electorate for the first time in almost 25 years.

Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson. Dominic Lorrimer

“Which is not to downplay it. It is a serious situation, but what it reflects is the need for us to be bigger, better, bolder, confident Liberals defining the future of the country,” he told the ABC’s Insiders.

Asked how last night’s vote should reflect on Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, Wilson said: “It shows that there’s a lot of work we’ve got to do, and Angus has been very upfront about that.”

Wilson said Labor should also take a lesson from the Liberal wipeout.

“One of the most consistent messages [from Farrer was] people want somebody who’s going to fight for them and for their future … and people are going to be very antagonistic towards the government breaking promises on tax issues.”
